Chapter 7: Trust and Leadership—Modeling, Multiplying, and Measuring Trust.
When you really think about it, leadership is all about trust. Leaders are handed resources, people, and a vision to move forward. Their real power? It comes from the trust they build and nurture every day. In organizations where trust runs high, leaders don’t just talk about trust—they show it, moment by moment, in everything they do.
So, what does it actually mean to model trust? Well, it’s about being open with your decisions, owning up to mistakes, and making sure credit is shared where it’s due. It also means setting the same expectations for yourself as you do for everyone else—and sticking to them, consistently and fairly. When leaders truly walk the talk, it’s contagious. People notice, they start to mirror that behavior, and before long, trust starts to ripple through the whole organization.
But modeling trust is just the beginning. Multiplying trust means setting up everyday systems and habits that make trust the default, not the exception. Think about it: Are you having regular, real conversations about goals and challenges? Are expectations clear, and is everyone being measured in a fair way? Trust grows even more when you recognize people for building trust—maybe it’s a shoutout, a reward, or simply a heartfelt thank you. And of course, there need to be safe spaces for feedback or even disagreement, so people know their voices matter.
Now, you might wonder, “How do you actually measure trust?” Even though trust might feel a bit intangible, it’s definitely something you can track. Surveys, feedback sessions, and just paying close attention to how people interact can tell you a lot. When trust is high, you’ll see open conversations, people sticking around, and real energy in the workplace. But if trust is lacking, watch for secrecy, lots of conflict, or folks resisting change.
Here’s a simple checklist leaders can use to get a sense of the trust climate:
Do people feel safe sharing their ideas and concerns? Are mistakes handled as chances to learn, or something to hide? Is information shared quickly and openly? And, are promises kept—or do they get broken more often than not?
If leaders check in on these questions regularly, it’s much easier to spot trouble early—and do something about it before it grows.
Let’s bring this to life with a real story. Imagine a CEO who invites the whole company to a monthly "ask me anything" session. No topics are off limits. And when tough questions come up? The CEO answers honestly, even if the news isn’t great. Over time, employees start to feel respected, included, and part of something bigger. That’s how a culture of trust is built—one honest conversation at a time.
